At least 28 Wirrayaraay men, women and children

content.p: On the evening of Sunday 10 June 1838, a party of twelve armed stockmen rode onto Myall Creek station in northern New South Wales, tied up a camp of Wirrayaraay people who had sought shelter there, and led them away to be killed. Most of the dead were women, children and older men. The Wirrayaraay are a clan of the Kamilaroi, or Gamilaraay, nation. The remains were later found burned, and the National Museum of Australia says the final death toll has never been confirmed.

The killings were not unusual for the frontier. What made Myall Creek exceptional was what followed. The case was reported, a magistrate investigated, and the colony's Attorney-General took eleven men to trial. The first jury acquitted them. The second convicted seven, and on 18 December 1838 those seven were hanged in Sydney. A state history museum's record of the first report describes it as the first time white men were hanged over the killing of Aboriginal people, while noting that a convict, John Kirby, had been executed in 1820 for the murder of a Newcastle chief. The man who led the party, John Henry Fleming, was never brought to court.

The National Museum of Australia says that by the 1830s violence on the New South Wales frontier was so widespread that the killing of Aboriginal people by stockmen, settlers and convicts was generally accepted, even though British law made it a capital crime. Edward Denny Day, the police magistrate at Muswellbrook, who later investigated Myall Creek, called the conflict in the Gwydir district "a war of extermination". Mark Tedeschi, a senior Crown prosecutor writing in Inside History, reports that Day described a campaign in which parties of armed stockmen repeatedly pursued Aboriginal people along the Gwydir River.

The summer of 1837 to 1838 was especially violent. SBS records that four settlers were killed on the Liverpool Plains in 1837 and that the acting governor sent troops. The National Museum of Australia adds that Major James Nunn of the Mounted Police led a punitive expedition and that on 26 January 1838 he and his men killed up to 50 Aboriginal people at Waterloo Creek.

Myall Creek station lay about 550 kilometres north of Sydney, according to SBS, and belonged to Henry Dangar, a surveyor who by 1850 held more than 300,000 acres, Tedeschi writes. Dangar was an absentee owner. The station had three huts for the manager and for the assigned convicts who worked there.

By the mid-1830s, the National Museum of Australia says, conflict had greatly reduced the Wirrayaraay population. In May 1838 a group sought refuge at Myall Creek. Tedeschi counts more than 40 people, SBS about 35, and says they had been invited by Charles Kilmeister, an assigned convict stockman. Tedeschi writes that they had previously lived peacefully for months at two other stations, McIntyre's and Wiseman's. The arrangement suited both sides: the Wirrayaraay had a respite from violence while the men helped stockmen with their work, and, the museum says, the station hands and Kilmeister in particular were on friendly terms with them. Some of the names the stockmen used survive in court depositions, among them Old Joey, King Sandy, Martha, Charley, Heppita, Tommy and Daddy.

Several days before the attack, Tedeschi says, ten of the most able-bodied men went to work at another station, Newton's, about 24 kilometres away. That left mainly older men, women and children at Myall Creek. The station manager, William Hobbs, was away at another of Dangar's properties, so only two assigned convicts, Kilmeister and the hut keeper George Anderson, were there, along with two teenage Aboriginal servants.

Tedeschi writes that the stockmen were in a murderous state of mind over what he calls depredations down the river days earlier; according to one account he cites, they had found speared and dying cattle. He says the people camped at Myall Creek could not possibly have had anything to do with them. The group that arrived that Sunday afternoon was, in his count, eleven mounted men led by John Henry Fleming; the full party, with Kilmeister, made twelve. Eleven were assigned convicts or former convicts. Fleming, then about 22 and an overseer near Moree, was the only free man who had never been a convict.

SBS reports that when the stockmen came, the Wirrayaraay ran into the station hut and asked for protection. Anderson asked the men what they wanted. They replied that they would "take them over the back of the range and frighten them". The group tied the people up and led them away from the camp. Anderson, who took no part, later described the terror of the people as they were led away, according to the National Museum of Australia. He heard two shots, SBS says, and when the men returned he saw their swords red with blood. The National Museum of Australia says two women and a young girl were set aside, another young girl was given to an Aboriginal stockman, and two boys escaped by jumping into the creek.

The ten men who had been away cutting bark came back that night and learned what had happened. According to SBS, the stockmen first went after them, failed to find them, then returned and burned the bodies. The Australian government's heritage listing and the Guardian give the number of dead differently: "approximately 30" and "at least 28" respectively. In sentencing, Justice Burton would later speak of "not less than 30 human souls".

Tedeschi quotes a family tradition among Fleming's descendants, in which Fleming claimed he fired once, to frighten a man, and that every man with a gun then fired. Tedeschi writes that Fleming's later account "bears no resemblance to the facts" and calls it an outright fabrication. It is recorded here as a family story, not as established fact.

The National Museum of Australia says three people set justice in motion: Hobbs, the local police superintendent Thomas Foster, and the settler Frederick Foot. A letter from Hobbs held by a state history museum says that on returning to the station after a few days away he saw "the remains of about thirty Blacks principally Women and Children" and was told that a party of white men had taken them away and destroyed nearly all of them. He wrote that he had not reported sooner because circumstances prevented him. The museum notes that he became a main Crown witness.

The new governor, Sir George Gipps, ordered Day to investigate. Day found partly burned bone fragments, took depositions from 19 witnesses and arrested eleven of the twelve men. Fleming fled. Tedeschi says that by the time Day arrested the eleven, colonial opinion was divided: a clear majority regarded Aboriginal people as "lawless savages" to be driven from the land, and only a small minority saw a chance for justice.

The eleven men stood trial in the Supreme Court in Sydney on 15 November 1838, before Chief Justice Sir James Dowling and a jury of twelve settlers. Plunkett prosecuted. SBS says landowners on the Liverpool Plains, among them Dangar, paid for a defence team. The National Museum of Australia says a group of landowners it calls the Black Association is alleged to have intimidated witnesses and advised jurors to stay away. Tedeschi says the charges were the murder of one man called Daddy and of an unnamed Aboriginal man.

Dowling told the jury that a most grievous offence had been committed and that "the life of a Black is as precious and valuable in the eyes of the law as that of the highest noble in the land". The prosecution rested on a burned skeleton identified as Daddy's, but no witness, including Anderson, could swear the remains were his. The jury acquitted all eleven. Tedeschi says they deliberated for 15 minutes; the National Museum says less than 20.

The Sydney Herald supported the accused. In the passage Tedeschi quotes, it wrote that "the whole gang of black animals are not worth the money the colonists will have to pay for printing the silly court documents".
content.h2: The second trial and the hangings
content.p: Plunkett refused to accept the acquittals. He held the men in gaol and brought a new charge, the murder of an Aboriginal child, which Tedeschi observes would not happen today. The National Museum of Australia says he split the men into a group of seven and a group of four, hoping they would give evidence against one another. It also says that arguments over whether they could be retried took place the day after a postponement on 26 November.

The second trial opened on 29 November before Justice Burton. Tedeschi writes that so many men summoned for jury service failed to appear that there were not enough to make a full jury. The trial lasted a day and a half. After an hour, the foreman announced "not guilty", but a juror at once said the real verdict was guilty, and after an inquiry the judge entered guilty verdicts. Three judges heard argument on 5 December and upheld Burton's rulings. Burton then sentenced all seven to death. In his remarks he said no provocation had been given and that the victims were slaughtered in the cool blood of "a poor defenceless tribe".

The seven were hanged at Sydney Gaol on the morning of 18 December 1838. Tedeschi says it was later reported that all had confessed their guilt at the gallows. One of them was Kilmeister. A Sydney resident, J.H. Bannatyne, wrote to a relative in England in a letter dated 17 December, now held by the State Library of New South Wales, that the trial had "created an extraordinary sensation in the Colony". He had come back from watching the hanging feeling "quite sick". The Australian Museum, which displays the letter, reads it as showing that people at the time thought killing Aboriginal people wrong.

The four men who had been separated from the seven, John Blake, James Lamb, George Palliser and Charles Toulouse, were to face a trial in which a witness named Yintayintin was to testify. The National Museum of Australia says that trial never took place because he disappeared in unexplained circumstances, and the four went free in February 1839.

The colony was not united behind the verdict. The National Museum says colonists were more outraged by the hanging of British subjects than by the massacre. SBS reports that the Sydney Morning Herald called the executions "judicial murder", while The Australian wrote that "the interests of humanity, the character of the colony and the honour of the British are outraged".

SBS and the National Museum say the case did not end frontier killing. SBS says some attacks went underground, with poisoned flour or water and better concealment of bodies. The Commonwealth heritage listing calls the case the colonial administration's first and last attempt to use the law against frontier killing, and the last time it ensured the law was applied equally to Aboriginal people and settlers.

The people involved had different fates. Hobbs lost his job with Dangar and, the museum says, had difficulty finding work. Blake died by suicide in 1852; his descendant Des Blake has said, "Did he have a guilty conscience? We like to think he did." Fleming went home to the Hawkesbury district. Tedeschi found that he died at 78 in August 1894, was a church warden and Justice of the Peace, and had a large funeral. Tedeschi calls the only hint of his past in the newspaper obituary a mention that he told stories of "the trouble he had with the Blacks". The National Museum says that his standing as a settler let him hide and return to society despite a reward for his capture. Tedeschi says the family story of how he avoided arrest is likely to be as inaccurate as the family account of the killings.

A memorial on the Bingara-Delungra Road, built by Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people working together, was opened on 10 June 2000. Its plaque honours the Wirrayaraay people "murdered on the slopes of this ridge in an unprovoked but premeditated act", and ends with a line in language as well as English. The Uniting Church says it grew from a gathering in 1998 organised by the church and led by Rev. John Brown and Aunty Sue Blacklock; the Friends of Myall Creek committee formed that year, the Guardian says.

The site went on the National Heritage List on 7 June 2008, when Environment Minister Peter Garrett called it "a sign of how we continue to grow and mature as a nation", and on the NSW heritage register in 2010. A service is held each year on the Sunday of the June long weekend. Descendants of victims, survivors and perpetrators attend: Blacklock, Elizabeth Connors and Lyall Munro on one side, Beulah Adams and Des Blake on the other, the National Museum says. For the 180th anniversary in 2018, the Inverell Times reported, a short video promoting plans for an education and cultural centre at the site was to be screened.

In 2019 the artist Ben Quilty, with the backing of Blacklock and Munro, made a painting of the site. In October 2021 New South Wales police investigated damage to the memorial: a plaque was scratched, a handrail stolen and a racist slogan marked into the ground, damage police believed took place between July and September.

On 9 June 2023, ahead of the 185th anniversary, the Sydney Morning Herald published an apology for its 1838 coverage. It said its stance had been shaped "not due to a lack of evidence or genuine doubts over the integrity of any legal process, but because the perpetrators were white and the dead black".
